content: Higher rates of early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) detection and improved three-year survival rates have been observed in individuals undergoing active surveillance. Although the role of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in HCC screening has been debated, recent guidelines recommend combining ultrasound with AFP testing, as this combination achieves a sensitivity of 63% for detecting early-stage HCC. Additionally, new blood-based biomarkers, such as DNA methylation assays (e.g., OncoGuard Liver), proteomic, glycomic (e.g., GlycoTest), and metabolomic markers, are being developed to enhance HCC screening. The most significant risk factors for developing HCC include cirrhosis, hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) positivity, persistently high HBV DNA levels, a family history of HCC, age over 40 years (reflecting prolonged infection and liver damage), elevated ALT levels (>45 U/L), and co-infections with HIV or HCV. Ethnicity also plays a role, with individuals of African or Asian descent being at higher risk. Other contributing factors include neonatal or childhood HBV infection, specific HBV genotypes (e.g. Risk calculators have been developed to predict HCC risk in individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using clinical and laboratory data, such as age, sex, albumin, bilirubin, ALT levels, HBeAg status, HBV DNA levels, and cirrhosis. Examples include the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer staging system and the GAG-HCC risk score. Recent models incorporate transient elastography as a substitute for HBV DNA levels, improving the performance of tools like the LSM-HCC and mREACH-B scores. Emerging biomarkers, such as HBcrAg, may also aid in risk assessment. Routine HCC surveillance using ultrasound and AFP every six months is recommended for high-risk individuals, as it enables early detection and improves survival through timely treatment. The benefits of screening outweigh potential harms, such as false positives or unnecessary interventions. Surveillance is particularly critical in lowand middle-income countries, where HCC often presents at advanced stages due to limited access to healthcare resources. Antiviral therapy plays a crucial role in reducing HCC risk and improving outcomes, even in individuals with HCC. Lifelong nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis to prevent HBV reactivation and associated complications. Discontinuation of therapy may be considered in select cases, such as those without cirrhosis, with evidence of HBeAg loss and seroconversion, and persistently normal ALT and undetectable HBV DNA levels. However, close monitoring is essential to detect relapse and reinstitute treatment if necessary. Relapse rates after stopping antiviral therapy are high, ranging from 40% to 95% within one year, depending on treatment duration and response. Factors associated with relapse include cirrhosis, older age, shorter therapy duration, and higher pre-treatment HBV DNA levels. New biomarkers, such as HBV RNA and HBcrAg, may help identify individuals at higher risk of relapse. In resource-limited settings, long-term antiviral therapy is often necessary due to limited access to HBV DNA monitoring. Generic tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is widely available at low cost in many lowand middle-income countries, making it a viable option for long-term management. However, the ability to monitor HBV replication and disease progression remains a challenge in these settings, emphasizing the need for improved access to diagnostic and treatment resources.
